steps.body: Real problems tell you which place to round to. "Nearest dollar" means round to the ones place — and the **tenths** digit (the dimes) is the decider. So $4.60 rounds to $5, because 6 is 5 or more. The context names the place; the rule stays the same.

numericErrors.feedback: $5 rounds up, but the tenths digit (dimes) is 4 — below 5 — so $4.40 rounds down to $4.
$4.40 is the exact price. Rounded to the nearest dollar, the tenths digit 4 keeps it at $4.

steps.body: "Nearest tenth" shows up in measurements — a length to the nearest tenth of a meter, a time to the nearest tenth of a second. Target the tenths place; the **hundredths** digit decides. The context changes; the decider-one-place-right rule does not.

explanationVariants: The hundredths digit 6 is 5 or more, so 2.36 m rounds up to 2.4 m.

numericErrors.feedback: 2.3 rounds down, but the hundredths digit 6 is 5 or more — so 2.36 rounds up to 2.4.
2 rounds to the nearest whole meter. To the nearest tenth, 2.36 rounds to 2.4.

steps.body: Let the context name the place.
takeaways: Word problems tell you the target place: nearest dollar (ones), nearest dime or tenth, nearest hundredth.
Whatever the target, the decider is the digit one place to its right.
5 or more rounds up, 4 or less stays — the same rule in every context.
